questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a group of assistive personnel about the chain of infection. Which of the following is an example of a reservoir?

options.rationale: A reservoir is where an infectious agent lives, grows, and replicates. Inanimate reservoirs include IV fluids, medical equipment, food, water, and soil.
This is the infectious agent itself, not the habitat where it lives and grows.
A cough is how a pathogen leaves the body, which makes it a portal of exit.
A break in the skin gives a pathogen a way into the body, which makes it a portal of entry.

questions.prompt: A nurse is planning care to protect a client from infection. Which actions break the chain of infection at the susceptible host link? Move the correct actions to the answer box.

options.text: Administer the client's annual influenza vaccine
options.rationale: Immunizations increase the host's defenses and decrease susceptibility to infection.

options.text: Encourage meals with adequate protein and calories
options.rationale: Proper nutrition strengthens the host's line of defense against infection.

options.text: Monitor and help control the client's blood glucose
options.rationale: Blood sugar control is one of the ways to decrease host susceptibility.

options.text: Apply a dressing over a draining wound
options.rationale: Containing drainage breaks the chain at the portal of exit, not the susceptible host.
Sterilization destroys the infectious agent; it does not strengthen the host.

options.text: Clean the bedside table with a hospital-grade disinfectant
options.rationale: Cleaning surfaces removes an inanimate reservoir; it does not strengthen the host.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who has a large amount of drainage from an abdominal wound. Which action breaks the chain of infection at the portal of exit?

options.text: Use a dressing to contain the drainage
options.rationale: Containing body fluids with drains or dressings keeps the pathogen from leaving the reservoir, which breaks the chain at the portal of exit.
Immunizations break the chain at the susceptible host link.

options.text: Apply lotion to the client's dry skin
options.rationale: Moisturizing keeps the skin barrier intact, which helps prevent a portal of entry. It does not contain drainage leaving the body.

options.text: Sterilize the equipment used for wound care
options.rationale: Sterilization destroys the infectious agent; it does not address how the pathogen leaves the client.

questions.prompt: A client has an indwelling urinary catheter. The nurse recognizes that the catheter represents which link in the chain of infection?

options.rationale: Invasive devices such as urinary catheters create a direct route for pathogens to travel into the body, in this case the bladder.
The infectious agent is the organism (bacteria, virus, fungus, parasite, or prion), not the device.
Mode of transmission is how the pathogen moves from place to place, such as contact, droplet, or airborne.
The client is the susceptible host. The catheter is the opening the pathogen uses to get in.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing several client records. Which clients have factors that increase their susceptibility to infection? Select all that apply.

options.text: A client who takes a proton pump inhibitor daily
options.rationale: Gastric acid suppressants such as proton pump inhibitors increase host susceptibility.

options.text: A client who is receiving radiation therapy
options.rationale: Radiation therapy increases susceptibility to infection.

options.text: A client who has a central venous catheter
options.rationale: Indwelling devices such as central venous catheters increase susceptibility by providing a portal of entry.

options.text: A client who takes a corticosteroid for asthma
options.rationale: Corticosteroids suppress the immune response and increase susceptibility.

options.text: A client who had hip replacement surgery 2 days ago
options.rationale: Recent surgery and an artificial joint both increase susceptibility to infection.

options.text: A client who eats a balanced diet and sleeps well
options.rationale: Good nutrition and adequate sleep support immunity and decrease susceptibility.

questions.prompt: A nasal swab shows MRSA in a client who has no manifestations of infection. The nurse should recognize that the client is

options.rationale: Colonization means the agent lives in the body, temporarily or permanently, without causing problems.

options.text: in the prodromal stage of infection.
options.rationale: The prodromal stage includes nonspecific manifestations such as fever and malaise. This client has none.

options.text: unable to transmit the organism to others.
options.rationale: A person can be a reservoir without showing disease and still pass the pathogen to new hosts.
Having no manifestations does not mean the client is immune; the organism is present in the body.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing how pathogens spread on the unit. Which situations are examples of indirect contact transmission? Move the correct situations to the answer box.

options.text: Wound drainage gets on a bed rail that staff then touch
options.rationale: Indirect contact occurs when a contaminated object sits between the infected person and the next person.

options.text: A nurse wears the same gloves while caring for two clients
options.rationale: Reusing PPE between clients carries the pathogen from one client to another through a contaminated item.

options.text: A shared blood pressure cuff is not disinfected between clients
options.rationale: Equipment shared between clients without proper cleaning transmits pathogens indirectly.

options.text: A client's blood splashes into an open cut on a nurse's hand
options.rationale: This is direct contact, because the pathogen moves straight from the infected person to another person.

options.text: A client sneezes and large droplets land in a visitor's mouth
options.rationale: This is droplet transmission into the mucosa of another host.

options.text: Many people become ill after eating the same contaminated produce
options.rationale: A common contaminated source that sickens many people is vehicle transmission.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who has pertussis and is coughing frequently. The nurse should understand that droplets from the client can transmit infection to others within which distance?

options.rationale: Droplets released by coughing and sneezing can transmit infection to others within 3 to 6 feet.
Droplets travel farther than this. Coughing and sneezing disperse them into the air around the client.

options.text: Throughout the unit, including outside the client's room
options.rationale: Particles that stay suspended and travel long distances describe airborne transmission, not droplet.
Spread through touch is contact transmission. Droplets travel through the air.

questions.prompt: Which client should the nurse place in an airborne infection isolation room?

options.text: A client who has suspected pulmonary tuberculosis
options.rationale: TB is transmitted by the airborne route, so the client needs a private negative-pressure room.
Influenza requires droplet precautions. It can be airborne under certain conditions, but droplet precautions are adequate and a negative-pressure room is not required.

options.text: A client who has C. difficile
options.rationale: C. difficile requires contact precautions.
Adenovirus requires droplet precautions.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about the body's defenses against infection. Which physical and chemical barriers should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.rationale: The skin is the body's largest organ and primary physical defense.
The GI (gastrointestinal) tract secretes acids and enzymes that destroy or neutralize some invaders.
Moist mucous membranes trap organisms. Dryness weakens this barrier, which is why oxygen is humidified.
Fever is a body-wide response to infection, not a physical or chemical barrier.
Antibodies are part of specific immunity.
Neutrophils are phagocytes that are part of nonspecific immunity.

questions.prompt: A client who is receiving oxygen through a nasal cannula reports that their nose feels dry. Which intervention should the nurse implement?

options.rationale: Humidification keeps the mucous membranes moist. Dry membranes can crack and allow micro-organisms to enter.
A higher flow would not relieve dryness and would require a prescription.

options.text: Remove the cannula for 1 hour each shift
options.rationale: Interrupting prescribed oxygen therapy is unsafe and does not address dryness.

options.text: Clean the nares with alcohol pads
options.rationale: Alcohol dries and irritates the mucous membranes, increasing the risk of cracking.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a client about how the body fights infection. Which role of phagocytes should the nurse include?

options.rationale: Phagocytes, such as neutrophils and macrophages, engulf and destroy micro-organisms.
Antibody production is part of specific immunity.
Physical barriers include the skin and mucous membranes, not phagocytes.
Phagocytes protect the body, which decreases susceptibility.

questions.prompt: A nurse is teaching a group of nursing students about nonspecific (innate) immunity. Which items are part of nonspecific immunity? Move the correct answers to the answer box.

options.rationale: Neutrophils are phagocytes released during the inflammatory response as part of nonspecific immunity.
Macrophages are phagocytes that make up nonspecific immunity along with neutrophils.
B cells are lymphocytes, which are part of specific immunity.
T cells are lymphocytes, which are part of specific immunity.
Antibodies (immunoglobulins) are part of specific immunity.
Intact skin is a physical barrier, a separate category of body defense.

questions.prompt: A nurse is assessing a client's surgical incision on postoperative day 3. Which findings are manifestations of inflammation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Skin around the incision is warm to the touch
options.rationale: Heat is one of the five cardinal signs of inflammation.
Redness is one of the five cardinal signs of inflammation.
Swelling is one of the five cardinal signs of inflammation.

options.text: Client reports pain at the site
options.rationale: Pain is one of the five cardinal signs of inflammation.
Loss of function is one of the five cardinal signs of inflammation.
Inflammation causes redness from increased blood flow, not pallor.
Inflammation causes heat at the site, not coolness.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for several clients who have inflammation. Which triggers of inflammation are noninfectious? Move the correct answers to the answer box.

options.rationale: Burns are a physical noninfectious trigger.
Frostbite is a physical noninfectious trigger.
Alcohol is a chemical noninfectious trigger.
Damaged cells are a biological noninfectious trigger.
Excitement is a psychological noninfectious trigger.
Bacteria are an infectious trigger.
Viruses are an infectious trigger.
Fungi are other micro-organisms, which are infectious triggers.

questions.prompt: A client who scraped their knee reports being unable to bend it because of swelling. The nurse documents this as which manifestation of inflammation?

options.rationale: Being unable to use or move the area normally is loss of function, one of the five cardinal signs.
Heat is warmth radiating from the area, not difficulty moving it.
Redness is a color change at the site, not difficulty moving it.
Pain is a separate cardinal sign. The client's inability to bend the knee describes loss of function.

questions.prompt: A client reports a fever, body aches, poor appetite, and fatigue for 1 day. No manifestations specific to a disease are present yet. The nurse identifies that the client is in which stage of infection?

options.rationale: The prodromal stage brings initial nonspecific manifestations such as fever, aches, poor appetite, and malaise.
During incubation the client has no manifestations yet.
In acute illness, manifestations specific to the disease become obvious.
Convalescence is the return to a previous or new balanced state of health.

questions.prompt: A client was exposed to an infectious agent 2 days ago and has no manifestations. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "You may be in the incubation stage. Lab tests can sometimes detect changes before symptoms appear."
options.rationale: Incubation lasts from exposure until the first symptom. Changes may be detectable through lab or diagnostic tests before symptoms start.

options.text: "Since you have no symptoms, you were not infected."
options.rationale: A client can be infected and in the incubation stage without symptoms.

options.text: "You are in the period of decline."
options.rationale: Decline follows acute illness, when manifestations subside.

options.text: "The incubation period always lasts exactly 2 weeks."
options.rationale: The incubation period differs for each agent and can last seconds, minutes, hours, days, or weeks.

questions.prompt: A client's localized skin infection has spread into the bloodstream. Which treatment should the nurse anticipate?

options.rationale: A systemic infection starts locally and spreads through the bloodstream. It requires IV antibiotics and careful monitoring.
Topical antibiotics can treat local infections but are not enough for a systemic infection.
Antihistamines block histamine to reduce swelling; they do not treat infection.

options.text: No treatment, because the infection will resolve on its own
options.rationale: A systemic infection affects the entire body and needs prompt treatment.

questions.prompt: A client's WBC count is 16,000/mm³. The nurse interprets this finding as

options.rationale: The expected WBC range is 5,000 to 10,000/mm³. An increased count indicates inflammation or infection.
16,000/mm³ is above the expected range of 5,000 to 10,000/mm³.
Neutropenia is an abnormally low count, not a high one.

options.text: showing a decreased ability to fight infection.
options.rationale: A decreased ability to fight infection is shown by a WBC count below the expected range.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for several clients on a medical unit. In which situations should the nurse use soap and water instead of an alcohol-based hand rub? Select all that apply.

options.text: The nurse's hands are visibly soiled
options.rationale: Alcohol-based hand rubs are not effective on visibly soiled hands. Soap and water remove dirt and debris.

options.text: After removing gloves when caring for a client who has C. difficile
options.rationale: Alcohol-based products do not remove spores. Wash with soap and water immediately after removing gloves.

options.text: Before entering the room of a client on droplet precautions
options.rationale: An alcohol-based hand rub is preferred when hands are not visibly soiled and spores are not involved.

options.text: After taking a client's blood pressure
options.rationale: With no visible soil and no spores, an alcohol-based hand rub is appropriate.

options.text: Before applying gloves to obtain a throat culture
options.rationale: Hand hygiene is required here, but an alcohol-based hand rub is acceptable when hands are not visibly soiled.

questions.prompt: A nurse is washing their hands with soap and water. For how long should the nurse rub the hands together?

options.text: At least 20 seconds, about the time it takes to sing "Happy Birthday" twice
options.rationale: Scrubbing for at least 20 seconds creates enough friction to remove micro-organisms.
This is not enough time to remove micro-organisms from all hand surfaces.
Water temperature should be adjusted before washing. It is not a measure of washing time.
This exceeds the recommended time for routine handwashing and can dry the skin.

questions.prompt: A nurse is reviewing medical and surgical asepsis with staff. Which activities require surgical asepsis? Move the correct activities to the answer box.

options.rationale: Catheter insertion is an invasive procedure that requires sterile technique.
Central line insertion requires maximal sterile barriers and aseptic technique.

options.text: Adding supplies to a sterile field
options.rationale: Items placed on a sterile field must remain sterile, which is surgical asepsis.

options.text: Performing hand hygiene before and after client care
options.rationale: Routine hand hygiene is medical asepsis (clean technique).

options.text: Preparing oral medications in a clean area
options.rationale: Keeping medication preparation areas clean is medical asepsis.
Isolation precautions are an example of medical asepsis.

questions.prompt: A nurse is opening a sterile package to set up a sterile field. Which flap should the nurse open first?

options.text: The flap farthest from the nurse's body
options.rationale: Opening the far flap first prevents the nurse from reaching over the sterile field later.

options.text: The flap closest to the nurse's body
options.rationale: The closest flap is opened last. Opening it first would mean reaching over the field to open the others.
The side flaps are opened second, one at a time, after the far flap.

options.text: Whichever flap is easiest to reach
options.rationale: Sterile packages are opened in a set order (far, sides, near) to prevent contamination.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing reusable surgical instruments for a sterile procedure. Which process eliminates all micro-organisms, including bacterial spores?

options.rationale: Sterilization eradicates all micro-organisms, including spores, through thermal, chemical, or radiation methods.
Low-level disinfection destroys most vegetative bacteria, but some spores, fungi, and viruses may remain.
High-level disinfection eliminates almost all micro-organisms, but some spores remain.
Medical asepsis reduces the number of micro-organisms; it does not eliminate them.

questions.prompt: A nurse is preparing to administer oral medications to a client who is on contact precautions. Which PPE should the nurse don? Move the correct items to the answer box.

options.rationale: Contact precautions require a gown at minimum when entering the room.
Contact precautions require gloves at minimum when entering the room.
N95 respirators are for airborne precautions.
Surgical masks are for droplet precautions.
Goggles are needed only when splashing to the eyes is expected.
Face shields are needed only when splashing to the face is expected.

questions.prompt: A client who has influenza and is on droplet precautions needs to be transported to the radiology department. Which action should the nurse take?

options.text: Place a surgical mask on the client for transport
options.rationale: Clients on droplet precautions wear a mask when they leave their room to prevent spreading the infectious agent.

options.text: Place an N95 respirator on the client
options.rationale: N95 respirators are worn by staff for airborne precautions. A surgical mask is appropriate for the client.

options.text: Postpone the test until precautions are discontinued
options.rationale: Clients on precautions can leave the room for necessary care when they wear a mask.

options.text: Have the client wear a gown and gloves
options.rationale: A gown and gloves do not contain respiratory droplets. The client needs a mask.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who has suspected tuberculosis. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assign the client to an airborne infection isolation room
options.rationale: Clients on airborne precautions need a private negative-pressure room (AIIR).

options.text: Keep the door to the room closed
options.rationale: The door of an airborne precaution room should remain closed.

options.text: Wear a fit-tested N95 respirator when entering the room
options.rationale: An N95 or higher respirator, specially fitted to the wearer, is required before entering.

options.text: Have the client wear a mask when leaving the room
options.rationale: Clients on airborne precautions wear a mask outside their room to prevent transmission.

options.text: Wear a surgical mask when providing care
options.rationale: A surgical mask is not enough for airborne particles. An N95 or higher respirator is required.

options.text: Leave the door open to monitor the client
options.rationale: An open door allows airborne particles to escape the negative-pressure room.

questions.prompt: A nurse is removing PPE after caring for a client. Which item should the nurse remove first?

options.rationale: Gloves are the most contaminated item and are removed first, followed by goggles or face shield, gown, then mask.
The gown is removed after the gloves and the goggles or face shield.
The mask is removed last, by its ties or ear loops, before hand hygiene.
Goggles are removed second, after the gloves.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who had an allogenic hematopoietic stem cell transplant 1 week ago. Which action is appropriate?

options.text: Keep fresh and dried plants out of the client's room
options.rationale: Plants, fresh or dried, are typically prohibited in protective environments to reduce exposure to pathogens.

options.text: Place the client in a negative-pressure room
options.rationale: Protective isolation uses positive airflow with HEPA filtration to keep pathogens out. Negative pressure is for airborne precautions.

options.text: Encourage visits from family members who have cold symptoms
options.rationale: This client is immunocompromised and must be protected from exposure to infection.

options.text: Room the client with a client who has pneumonia
options.rationale: Rooming with an infected client would expose this immunocompromised client to pathogens.

questions.prompt: A nurse is stuck with a needle that was just used on a client. Which action should the nurse take first?

options.text: Wash the area with soap and water
options.rationale: Washing the exposed area with soap and water is the immediate first action after a needlestick.

options.text: Report the exposure to the charge nurse
options.rationale: The exposure must be reported immediately, but only after the area is washed.

options.text: Apply an antiseptic to the site
options.rationale: No research shows that antiseptics are more beneficial than soap and water.

options.text: Wait to see if the site becomes inflamed
options.rationale: Needlestick exposures need immediate action, reporting, and follow-up testing per protocol.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who has had an indwelling urinary catheter since surgery 3 days ago. Which action should the nurse take to help prevent a catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)?

options.text: Advocate for removal of the catheter as soon as it is no longer needed
options.rationale: Avoiding unnecessary catheterization and removing the catheter early are key CAUTI prevention measures.

options.text: Place the drainage bag on the floor
options.rationale: When the tubing or bag touches a contaminated surface, pathogens can migrate into the bladder.

options.text: Insert a catheter routinely for all postoperative clients
options.rationale: Unnecessary catheterization increases infection risk.

options.text: Disconnect the tubing to empty the bag
options.rationale: Breaking the closed system contaminates it. The system must stay aseptic.

questions.prompt: A client who has an MRSA infection asks the nurse what that means. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?

options.text: "It's a bacterium that is resistant to one or more classes of antimicrobials, which makes it challenging to treat."

options.text: "It's a virus that responds to any antibiotic."
options.rationale: MRSA is a bacterium (Staphylococcus aureus), and it is resistant to certain antimicrobials.

options.text: "It can only spread through the air."
options.rationale: MDROs are managed with contact precautions because they spread through direct and indirect contact.

questions.prompt: A newborn receives antibodies from the mother. The nurse identifies this as which type of immunity?

options.rationale: Antibodies from an outside source, such as maternal antibodies, provide passive immunity. It is temporary and has no memory.

questions.prompt: An older adult client in a residential facility has a urinary tract infection. Which finding should the nurse recognize as an atypical indication of infection in this client?

options.rationale: Older adults may show atypical signs such as confusion, agitation, or incontinence instead of typical findings.

questions.prompt: A nurse has prepared a sterile field. Which events contaminate the field? Select all that apply.

options.text: Sterile normal saline soaks through the drape

options.text: The provider drops a sterile instrument onto the near side of the field

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for several clients on a medical-surgical unit. Which action is the best way for the nurse to prevent health care–associated infections?

options.text: Perform frequent and effective hand hygiene

options.text: Administer prophylactic antibiotics to all clients

options.text: Place all clients on contact precautions

options.text: Wear an N95 respirator for all care

options.rationale: Isolate the client until the vesicles have crusted over.

options.text: Administer the recombinant zoster vaccine to treat the rash

options.rationale: Cool water compresses or a cool bath are recommended.

questions.prompt: A nurse is caring for a client who has an infection. Which findings indicate the infection is systemic rather than localized? Move the correct findings to the answer box.
